entry.title: Incremental Computation Graphs Overview
entry.content:
Lobsters Top | dziban.net | discussion

Incremental computation graphs use mutable inputs and pure, memoized functions to track dependencies and minimize redundant execution during development tasks like code compilation and type-checking. Developed as part of the Yabu programming language project and inspired by Salsa, the system builds a runtime dependency graph where computations are dynamically linked to their source inputs.

When an input changes, a red-green walk algorithm checks revision timestamps along the dependency chain, invalidating only the affected computations while returning cached results for everything else. This selective invalidation allows compilers and typecheckers to operate at interactive speeds even across large codebases.

entry.title: Software Is Slow Because of Bad Design, Not Slow Languages
entry.content:
Lobsters Top | seangoedecke.com | discussion | hacker news

Sean Goedecke argues that rewriting software in faster languages like Rust or C rarely yields dramatic performance improvements because most real-world programs are I/O-bound rather than CPU-bound. Since a significant portion of execution time is spent waiting on databases, networks, or disks, speeding up code execution leaves the primary bottlenecks untouched. Furthermore, high-level languages already delegate heavy computational workloads to tightly optimized libraries written in lower-level languages.

Significant software speedups typically stem from architectural redesigns that minimize unnecessary work, such as caching slow API calls, executing operations asynchronously or in parallel, and resolving N+1 database query problems. While language choice matters for specific CPU-bound hotspots, prioritizing system design offers far greater performance gains than code translation alone.

entry.title: Raymond Chen Examines Why x86 Uses Ud2 Instead of Int 6
entry.content:
Lobsters Top | devblogs.microsoft.com | discussion

Raymond Chen explains why the x86 architecture relies on the ud2 instruction for undefined opcodes rather than manually invoking the int 6 software interrupt. Although both instructions are two bytes long, they trigger fundamentally different exception behaviors at the hardware level.

An invalid opcode generates a fault, which reports the address of the offending instruction to the exception handler so the system can inspect or attempt recovery. Conversely, a software interrupt like int 6 acts as a trap, pointing to the subsequent instruction and causing confusion in fault handlers that expect to analyze the invalid opcode. Furthermore, operating systems restrict user-mode programs from directly invoking int 6 in protected mode, making an actual undefined instruction necessary.
